services.name: Customer Onboarding Service
services.description: Orchestrates the end-to-end customer onboarding journey for both retail and commercial customers. Coordinates identity verification, KYC checks, product eligibility, account setup, and welcome communications across all channels. Acts as the process owner for the shared onboarding sub-capability spanning Retail and Commercial Banking.
technology_constraints: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(e): personal data collected during onboarding must be limited to what is necessary; data minimisation must be enforced at intake
FCA SYSC 6.1: firms must have adequate systems to identify, assess, monitor, and manage compliance risk during onboarding
Biometric identity verification providers must be ICO-registered data processors; contracts must include UK GDPR-compliant data processing agreements
Electronic identity verification must meet JMLSG Part I Chapter 5 standards to satisfy CDD obligations
Onboarding journey must be resumable across sessions: partial applications must be persisted for at least 30 days

design_decisions.decision: Implement onboarding as a durable, resumable workflow using SVC-055 (Workflow Engine), with each onboarding step as an independently completable task.
design_decisions.rationale: Customers frequently abandon onboarding mid-journey and return later. A durable workflow preserves state across sessions and channels, avoiding customers having to restart. It also provides an auditable process record for FCA supervision.
alternatives_considered: Session-based stateful UI with server-side session store
Event-driven choreography with no central orchestrator
design_decisions.rejected_because: Session stores are lost on session expiry and cannot survive channel switches; event-driven choreography without an orchestrator makes it impossible to determine what step a customer is on, breaking the FCA audit trail.

design_decisions.decision: Maintain a single canonical customer identity record created during onboarding, shared via SVC-100 (IAM), rather than separate identity records per product line.
design_decisions.rationale: Retail and commercial onboarding share identity verification. A single identity record prevents duplicate verification costs, enables FSCS SCV compliance, and ensures KYC data is consistent across CAP-001 and CAP-002.
alternatives_considered: Separate customer identity records per capability
Identity federation with eventual consistency sync
design_decisions.rejected_because: Separate records create divergence risk and double the identity verification cost; federated eventual consistency allows windows where KYC status is inconsistent across channels, creating regulatory risk.

services.name: Sanctions Screening Service
services.description: Provides real-time and batch sanctions screening against UK, EU, UN, OFAC, and other relevant sanctions lists. Screens customers, counterparties, payment beneficiaries, and beneficial owners. Manages list update ingestion, match scoring, and alert workflow for analyst review.
technology_constraints: OFSI and HM Treasury require screening against UK Consolidated List; updates must be reflected within 1 hour of list publication
Screening must be synchronous and blocking for all payment release decisions; it cannot be advisory or fire-and-forget
False positive rate must be managed below 1% to avoid operational paralysis, requiring fuzzy-matching algorithms with configurable sensitivity
OFAC 50% rule: beneficial ownership chains must be screened to entity level, not just direct counterparty
All screening decisions (match, no-match, override) must be retained for 5 years under UK MLR 2017

design_decisions.decision: Maintain an in-memory compiled screening index rebuilt from source lists on each update, with a read-only replica serving live traffic during rebuilds.
design_decisions.rationale: Synchronous screening at sub-100ms requires in-memory matching. The 1-hour update SLA requires hot-reload of list updates without service downtime; a read-only replica during rebuild prevents any screening gap.
alternatives_considered: Database-backed fuzzy matching
External SaaS screening API per transaction
design_decisions.rejected_because: Database fuzzy matching cannot meet sub-100ms synchronous SLA at payment volumes; external SaaS introduces a third-party availability dependency on a blocking, regulatory-critical path.

design_decisions.decision: Implement a tiered match confidence scoring system (definite, probable, possible) with only definite matches auto-blocking and lower tiers routed to analyst review queues.
design_decisions.rationale: Purely binary matching produces unacceptable false positive rates that block legitimate customer payments. Tiered confidence allows automated blocking of high-certainty matches while keeping the analyst queue manageable.
alternatives_considered: Binary exact/no-match only
All matches auto-blocked pending review
design_decisions.rejected_because: Binary exact matching misses name variations of sanctioned entities; all-block creates an unmanageable analyst queue that causes payment delays inconsistent with FPS SLAs.

services.name: Credit Decision Service
services.description: Provides centralised, policy-consistent credit decisioning for all lending products across retail and commercial banking. Integrates credit bureau data, internal behavioural data, and affordability models to produce credit decisions, limit assignments, and risk-based pricing inputs.
technology_constraints: FCA CONC rules: credit decisions must be based on a reasonable assessment of creditworthiness; income and expenditure assessment mandatory for consumer credit
GDPR Article 22 and FCA Consumer Duty: automated credit refusals must be explainable on request; the service must support human review of any adverse decision
Credit reference agency (CRA) data (Experian, Equifax, TransUnion) access subject to data sharing agreements; customer consent required for hard searches
PRA IRB model requirements: credit models used for regulatory capital must be independently validated and PRA-approved
Outcome monitoring: FCA Consumer Duty requires monitoring of credit decision outcomes across customer cohorts for evidence of poor outcomes

design_decisions.decision: Implement credit policy rules as a versioned, externally-managed decision table separate from the scoring engine, allowing policy changes without model redeployment.
design_decisions.rationale: Credit policy (e.g. minimum income thresholds, LTV limits) changes frequently in response to risk appetite decisions. Separating policy rules from the scoring engine means compliance/risk teams can update policy on a faster cycle than engineering releases.
alternatives_considered: Policy rules hard-coded in the scoring engine
Policy rules as configuration in the model registry
design_decisions.rejected_because: Hard-coded rules couple policy changes to engineering sprints; embedding policy in the model registry conflates credit policy governance with model risk governance.

design_decisions.decision: Log all input features and decision outputs to SVC-104 (Data Platform) for every credit decision, enabling outcome monitoring and model performance tracking.
design_decisions.rationale: FCA Consumer Duty and PRA model risk management both require ongoing monitoring of credit decision quality and fairness. Comprehensive decision logging in the Data Platform enables cohort analysis and model drift detection.
alternatives_considered: Sample-based logging for performance only
Log to service-local database
design_decisions.rejected_because: Sample-based logging is insufficient for FCA Consumer Duty outcome monitoring across all customer segments; service-local databases cannot support the cross-product analytics needed for portfolio-level monitoring.

services.name: Notification Service
services.description: Multi-channel customer and internal notification delivery service supporting push, SMS, email, in-app, and letter channel types. Manages notification templates, personalisation, delivery tracking, opt-out preferences, and regulatory delivery obligations.
technology_constraints: FCA BCOBS requires certain account notifications (e.g. unarranged overdraft) to be delivered before charges are applied; delivery timing must be evidenced
UK GDPR and PECR: marketing communications require opt-in consent; transactional notifications may rely on legitimate interests; consent state must be checked at send time
FCA Consumer Duty: notifications that prompt a customer action (e.g. contract renewal) must be delivered with adequate notice; delivery evidence must be retained
SMS and push notification delivery must use UK-regulated providers with sub-30-second delivery SLA for time-critical regulatory notifications
Notification content for regulated products must pass through a compliance sign-off workflow before template activation

design_decisions.decision: Separate notification intent (what to tell the customer and why) from channel execution (how and when to deliver) using an intent-based API consumed by domain services.
design_decisions.rationale: Domain services understand what event has occurred (e.g. payment received) but should not hardcode channel logic. The Notification Service owns channel routing, templating, and consent checking, allowing channels to be added or changed without domain service changes.
alternatives_considered: Each domain service calls channel providers directly
Shared notification table polled by a dispatcher
design_decisions.rejected_because: Direct channel calls create N×M coupling between domain services and channel providers; polled tables introduce delivery latency that violates regulatory timing requirements for BCOBS notifications.

design_decisions.decision: Check opt-out and consent preferences from SVC-100 (IAM) at the point of dispatch, not at the point of notification creation.
design_decisions.rationale: Customer preferences change between when a notification is raised and when it is dispatched (especially for queued or scheduled notifications). Checking at dispatch ensures the most current consent state is respected.
alternatives_considered: Embed consent check at notification creation in domain service
Cache consent state within Notification Service
design_decisions.rejected_because: Creation-time checks capture a stale consent state; a local cache can be stale for the cache TTL period, potentially sending a notification after a customer has opted out.

services.name: Document Management Service
services.description: Provides tamper-evident, auditable storage and retrieval of all regulated documents including onboarding evidence, KYC packs, credit assessments, customer communications, and regulatory submissions. Enforces retention schedules and supports legal hold.
technology_constraints: Documents must be stored as write-once, read-many (WORM) artefacts; post-storage modification must be technically impossible
FCA record-keeping: minimum retention periods vary by document type (6 years for most financial records, 5 years for AML, indefinite for some legal agreements)
Legal hold: documents under regulatory investigation must be exempt from retention-based deletion; legal hold flags must be applied and released by authorised personnel only
UK GDPR right to erasure: documents containing personal data must support a redaction mechanism where legally permissible; erasure must not be possible when in conflict with FCA retention obligations
Documents must be indexed for full-text search to support regulatory information requests and subject access requests within FCA/ICO mandated timelines

design_decisions.decision: Implement WORM storage using object store immutability policies (e.g. S3 Object Lock or equivalent) at the infrastructure layer, not application-layer controls.
design_decisions.rationale: Application-layer WORM controls can be bypassed by privileged users or application bugs. Infrastructure-layer immutability is enforced by the storage platform itself and is auditable by the cloud provider independently of the bank's application.
alternatives_considered: Application-layer append-only controls with privileged admin override
Cryptographic hash verification without storage immutability
design_decisions.rejected_because: Application-layer controls can be bypassed by database administrators; hash verification proves tampering has occurred but does not prevent it.

design_decisions.decision: Separate document metadata (index, retention schedule, legal hold status) from document content storage, with metadata in a queryable database and content in WORM object store.
design_decisions.rationale: Metadata must be queryable for regulatory searches and SAR responses; WORM object stores are not optimised for complex queries. Separation allows metadata to be updated (e.g. legal hold applied) without modifying the immutable content.
alternatives_considered: Store metadata within the document as a header
Single database with BLOB storage for content
design_decisions.rejected_because: Header metadata cannot be updated without creating a new document version; BLOB databases do not scale economically to the document volumes expected across all bank capabilities.

services.name: Workflow Engine
services.description: Provides durable, auditable, long-running workflow orchestration for complex multi-step business processes that span multiple services. Used for mortgage origination, trade finance instrument processing, and KYC/AML escalation workflows.
technology_constraints: Workflow state must survive service restarts and infrastructure failures; durability is a non-negotiable requirement
Human task steps (e.g. underwriter approval, KYC analyst review) must support SLA monitoring with escalation triggers
Audit trail: every workflow state transition must be timestamped and attributed to either a system actor or a named human actor
Workflows must support compensation (rollback) sequences for failed multi-step processes to maintain data consistency
Mortgage origination workflows can span weeks; the engine must support arbitrarily long-running process instances without memory leaks or state degradation

design_decisions.decision: Select a workflow engine that persists workflow state externally (e.g. Temporal or Conductor) rather than in-process memory, to guarantee durability across restarts.
design_decisions.rationale: Mortgage origination and trade finance workflows run for days to weeks. In-process state is lost on restart; only externally persisted workflow state provides the durability guarantee required for long-running regulatory processes.
alternatives_considered: BPM platform (e.g. Camunda) with its own persistence
Custom saga tables in domain service databases
design_decisions.rejected_because: BPM platforms are viable but introduce heavyweight BPMN tooling that is harder for engineering teams to version-control; custom saga tables are per-service and cannot provide cross-service workflow visibility needed for operational monitoring.

design_decisions.decision: Scope the Workflow Engine exclusively to complex, human-in-the-loop, or long-running processes; simple two-step automated flows must remain in-domain as service logic.
design_decisions.rationale: Centralising all orchestration in a workflow engine creates a bottleneck and couples unrelated domains. The engine is warranted only where durability, human tasks, or compensation sequences are required.
alternatives_considered: Use workflow engine for all inter-service coordination
Separate workflow engine per capability
design_decisions.rejected_because: Universal use creates unnecessary coupling and makes the engine a single point of failure for low-complexity flows; per-capability engines defeat the purpose of a shared cross-cutting service and create operational fragmentation.
